rubric.why: Checks that ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron.
rubric.description: State that energy is required to remove one electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the energy requirement and removal of one electron.

rubric.why: Checks the gaseous atom and positive ion involved in the first ionization process.
rubric.description: Identify the atom’s state and the positive ion formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the electron is removed from an isolated gaseous atom to form a positive ion.

modelAnswer: First ionization energy is the energy required to remove one electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
The atom forms a unipositive ion: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.

items.followUp: Write any three differences between Rutherford’s atomic model and Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Contrasts Rutherford’s unrestricted electron paths with Bohr’s permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Compare the orbits allowed in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford allowed any orbit whereas Bohr proposed permitted or fixed orbits.

rubric.why: Checks the contrast between Rutherford’s lack of definite energy levels and Bohr’s assigned energies.
rubric.description: Compare the energy levels in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model had no definite energy levels while Bohr assigned definite energies to permitted orbits.

rubric.why: Checks the stability problem in Rutherford’s model and Bohr’s stable stationary orbits.
rubric.description: Compare how the models account for atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Rutherford’s stability problem and Bohr’s stable orbits.

accept: could not explain the hydrogen line spectrum
rubric.why: Checks the models’ explanations of the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.description: Compare their explanation of the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford could not explain the spectrum and Bohr explained it using energy-level transitions.

rubric.why: Contrasts energy radiation by revolving electrons in Rutherford’s model with non-radiating Bohr stationary orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s revolving electrons would radiate or lose energy, whereas electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model allowed electrons to revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr proposed only certain permitted orbits.
Rutherford’s model had no definite electron energy levels; Bohr assigned a definite energy to each permitted orbit.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr’s stationary orbits made the atom stable.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the hydrogen line spectrum; Bohr’s model explained it using electron transitions between energy levels.
In Rutherford’s model, revolving electrons should radiate energy and lose it; in Bohr’s stationary orbits, electrons do not radiate energy.

items.followUp: Classify solutions as mixtures and give one example of each type of mixture.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a mixture as a physical combination of substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances.

rubric.why: Checks the classification and example of a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: Describe a homogeneous mixture and give an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its uniform composition and giving a valid example.

rubric.why: Checks the classification and example of a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: Describe a heterogeneous mixture and give an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its non-uniform composition and giving a valid example.

rubric.why: Checks characteristic properties of mixtures beyond their classification.
rubric.description: State that mixture components can be present in variable proportions and separated physically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both variable proportions and separation by physical methods.

modelAnswer: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances that are not chemically combined.
Its components can be present in variable proportions and can be separated by physical methods.
Homogeneous mixture: it has a uniform composition throughout; for example, salt solution.
Heterogeneous mixture: it has a non-uniform composition; for example, sand and water.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of an ionic bond in magnesium oxide (MgO).

rubric.why: Checks the electron arrangements that allow sodium to transfer one electron to chlorine.
rubric.description: Give the electronic configurations of sodium and chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Na = 2,8,1 and Cl = 2,8,7.

rubric.why: Checks the electron transfer from sodium to chlorine.
rubric.description: Explain the transfer of one electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium transfers or loses its outermost electron to chlorine, which gains it.

rubric.why: Checks that sodium and chlorine form the correct oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

rubric.why: Checks the force that holds the ions together and constitutes the ionic bond.
rubric.description: Explain what forms the ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Checks the ratio and formula of the ionic compound formed.
rubric.description: Name the compound and give its formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying sodium chloride as NaCl, formed in a 1:1 ratio.

modelAnswer: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, while chlorine has 2,8,7.
A sodium atom transfers its outermost electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium forms Na⁺ (2,8) and chlorine forms Cl⁻ (2,8,8), giving both ions stable outer shells.
The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond.
The ions combine in a 1:1 ratio to form sodium chloride, NaCl.
